passages.happening:
‘Then Hezekiah sent word throughout all Israel and Judah, and he also wrote letters to Ephraim and Manasseh inviting them to come to the house of the LORD in Jerusalem to keep the Passover of the LORD, the God of Israel’ (verse 1). Because the priests were not consecrated in time and the people had not gathered, they decide to keep it in the second month (verses 2-3), and the proclamation goes from Beersheba to Dan (verse 5).

The letters say, “Children of Israel, return to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, so that He may return to those of you who remain, who have escaped the grasp of the kings of Assyria” (verse 6). ‘For the LORD your God is gracious and merciful; He will not turn His face away from you if you return to Him’ (verse 9). The couriers go from city to city, ‘but the people scorned and mocked them’ (verse 10). Yet some from Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun humble themselves and come (verse 11), and in Judah God gives the people one heart to do what the king commanded (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
With the temple cleansed, Hezekiah turns to the people. Since the division after Solomon, the northern tribes had worshiped apart from Jerusalem, and many had now been deported by Assyria. His letters try to gather what remains of all Israel around the one house of God, the Chronicler's great hope on display.

The letter addresses those who escaped the kings of Assyria. Tiglath-pileser the Third had deported people from Galilee and Gilead around 732 BC, and Samaria fell in 722 BC. If Hezekiah began to reign around 715 BC, the northern kingdom no longer existed, and the letters went to a scattered remnant under Assyrian rule; if around 727 BC, the event might fall near Samaria's fall. Either way, sending couriers into Assyrian-held land was bold. Letters carried by royal couriers were the ordinary means of state communication.

The letter is built on one verb, shuv, to turn or return, repeated again and again: return to the LORD so that he may return to you; if you return, your captives will return. It echoes God's own description of himself to Moses, gracious, channun, and merciful. The response is mixed: mockery, humility, and in Judah a heart made one by God.
passages.later: God described himself to Moses as ‘The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness’ (Exodus 34:6).
passages.asks: The couriers were mocked, and some still came. Ask whether you have scorned an invitation back to God, or been scorned for carrying one. And ask whom you could invite home this year, whatever the answer.

passages.t: A Passover kept imperfectly, and God heals
passages.happening:
A very large assembly gathers in Jerusalem in the second month (verse 13). They remove the altars in Jerusalem and throw them into the Kidron Valley (verse 14). The Levites slaughter the Passover lambs for those who are not clean (verse 17). Many from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar and Zebulun ‘had not purified themselves, yet they ate the Passover, contrary to what was written’ (verse 18). Hezekiah prays, “May the LORD, who is good, provide atonement for everyone” (verse 18), ‘who sets his heart on seeking God’ (verse 19), even if not cleansed by the rules of the sanctuary. ‘And the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people’ (verse 20).

They keep the feast seven days with great joy, and then seven more (verses 21-23). ‘So there was great rejoicing in Jerusalem, for nothing like this had happened there since the days of Solomon son of David king of Israel’ (verse 26). The priests and Levites stand to speak God's favor over the people, ‘and God heard their voice, and their prayer came into His holy dwelling place in heaven’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Passover remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt and was kept on the fourteenth day of the first month, followed by the Feast of Unleavened Bread. The law allowed someone unclean or far away to keep it a month later, and Hezekiah applied that rule to the whole nation. Ritual purity mattered because contact with death, some illnesses and other conditions made a person unfit to eat holy food until cleansed. Many northerners had no experience of these rules after two centuries of separate worship, so the Levites slaughtered lambs on their behalf.

Second Kings does not mention this Passover, and it says of Josiah's later one that none like it had been kept since the judges. Some explain that Josiah's was unmatched in its strict keeping of the law, while Hezekiah's was irregular; others think the Chronicler drew on sources Kings did not use; some think he shaped the account to show Hezekiah as a new Solomon. The chapter ends with two prayers heard, Hezekiah's for the unclean and the priests' for the people, recalling Solomon's prayer that God would hear from heaven. Healed, rapha, may mean spared from sickness, or restored more widely.
passages.later: The law made room for a late Passover. If someone was ‘unclean because of a dead body’ (Numbers 9:10) or far from home, ‘he may still observe the Passover to the LORD’ (Numbers 9:10).
passages.hard:
If God gave detailed purity laws, why does he accept people who broke them here?

The text itself admits the irregularity: the people ate contrary to what was written. Hezekiah does not pretend the rules do not matter; he asks God to pardon those who seek him with their heart, levav. The LORD's answer shows that the law served the relationship rather than replacing it, a theme the prophets also press. Some interpreters stress that this was an exceptional act of mercy at a time of need, not a new rule, and that the priests and Levites still made sure the sacrifices were rightly handled. Others see an early instance of the principle that God looks on the heart. Both readings keep the tension the text keeps: the rules are real, and God's grace is greater.
passages.asks: People came who were not ready, and the king prayed for them, and God healed them. Ask whether you have stayed away from God because you were not clean enough to come. And ask whom you have kept at a distance because they did not know the rules.
